blocks.text: Daniel continues the established pattern of prayer described in verses 10–11 after the prohibition is signed. This can inform reflection on resistance to an imperial command, but the story does not supply one universal political rule: it does not authorize contempt for law, reckless exposure of others, or the expectation that faithful resistance will always end in miraculous rescue.

The chapter places Darius the Mede after Babylon’s fall. No ruler securely matching all of Daniel’s descriptions has been independently identified, and proposed identifications have not reached broad agreement. The identity of Darius therefore remains an open historical question rather than a settled detail.

Daniel survives in substantially different Old Greek and Theodotionic forms, with notable differences in chapters 4–6 and in the form and placement of additions. Differences between these versions need to be considered passage by passage; neither version-label by itself explains every variation.
